intro: This is Göbeklitepe, Enclosure D, from the second half of the 10th millennium BC. It is one of the oldest monumental structures known, and the earliest dated of the circles. Look at the two pillars at its centre. They have arms, hands and a belt: these stones are human in form, and they stand facing one another.
spot-1: Now you are looking at the central pillars. Two T-shaped stones, 5.5 m tall, face one another. Look closely and you will see they are human in form, with arms, hands and a belt.
spot-2: Now the camera turns to the ring of pillars. Twelve pillars are set around the circle, and every one of them is turned towards the centre.
spot-3: Here is the dry-stone wall. The gaps between the pillars are filled with unworked stone, so the pillars stand inside the wall itself.
spot-4: Now look down at the terrazzo floor. It was poured from burnt lime, and it is among the earliest floors of its kind known anywhere.
spot-5: And here is the bench, made for sitting, running around the inside of the wall. Imagine people seated here, facing the great stones.
uncertainty: Finally, what this model does not know. Published diameters for the enclosure range from 20 to 30 metres; the model takes 30. The animals on the pillars are not drawn by hand. Instead, photographs of the excavated reliefs are used as height maps and cut into the stone, so the depth is real and throws its own shadow. What is not real is which animal stood where on which pillar: the photographs come from the pillars of Enclosure C, while the model shows Enclosure D. The arms, hands, belt and loincloth of the two central stones are documented for D, and they are modelled as the low relief they are. Whether the circle was roofed is unknown, and the model leaves that question open.
